newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO-Russia summit may give Chirac election boost.
newsitem.headline: NATO-Russia summit may give Chirac election boost.

text.p: The Americans do the power-broking, the French do the catering. Welcome to the new NATO.

The ceremony to sign the Founding Act of a new NATO-Russia partnership in Paris on Tuesday will be the first NATO summit held in France since General Charles de Gaulle withdrew from the Atlantic alliance's military wing in 1966 and ordered it to remove its political and military headquarters from French soil.
President Jacques Chirac is hoping the glittering event will give him a sorely needed political boost between the two rounds of a parliamentary election on which his future power may hinge.
"It shows that under his leadership, France can play an important role in the new NATO," a presidential aide said.
But whether the summit will sway disgruntled French voters, who on Sunday cast more votes for the left-wing opposition than for Chirac's centre-right coalition, remains to be seen.

The ceremony at the Elysee presidential palace, in the presence of U.S. President Bill Clinton, Russian President Boris Yeltsin and almost all the leaders of the 16 NATO nations, will be broadcast live on French television.
The visiting dignitaries may be meeting a French leader about to become a virtual lame duck, forced to share power with a left-wing cabinet if the voting trend is repeated next Sunday.

Chirac will give Tuesday's keynote speech, stressing the historic nature of a pact laying the foundations of a new cooperative relationship between former Cold War adversaries, and erasing the division of Europe that followed the 1945 Yalta conference.

The French are particularly bitter about Yalta because they were excluded from the Crimean summit between U.S. president Franklin Roosevelt, Soviet leader Josef Stalin and British prime minister Winston Churchill in the last months of World War Two.
Foreign policy usually plays little part in French elections and signs are that voters were motivated by record unemployment, high taxes and stagnant purchasing power.

The president's attempt to use international diplomacy to influence the first round, using a visit by Chancellor Helmut Kohl last week to stress that France must "speak with one voice" to influence Europe, failed to impress the electorate.

The opposition Socialists and Communists, with whom Chirac may have to "cohabit" from next week, have criticised him for bringing France back closer to NATO without gaining anything in exchange from the United States.
Diplomats said it was safe to assume that if the left won, France's reintegration would be frozen at its current, semi-detached state.
In any case, the Paris summit will not resolve the question of whether or not France makes a full return to NATO's integrated military command.
Chirac launched a rapprochement with the alliance in December 1995, six months after his election.
But he has made a full return conditional on the United States handing over the key southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European officer.
Washington has refused to give up the Naples-based command, traditionally held by the admiral who commands the nuclear-armed U.S. Sixth Fleet, the largest naval force in the Mediterranean.
French and American diplomats have been trying to negotiate a compromise, but there is no agreement yet and the election campaign has effectively put the talks on hold.
French officials say the issue may be left until after a NATO summit in Madrid in July, which will invite the first former Communist central and eastern European countries to join.
